questions.q: In Microsoft Entra ID, which object is the single global definition of an application, living in the tenant where the app was registered?
options: The application object (app registration)
The service principal (enterprise application)
The OAuth2 permission grant
The managed identity
questions.explanation: An app has one application object in its home tenant. Each tenant that uses the app gets its own service principal (enterprise application), which the local admins control.

questions.q: Contoso registers a multitenant app. When the first user from Fabrikam signs in and consent is granted, what is created in Fabrikam's tenant?
options: A copy of the app registration that Fabrikam can edit independently
A new app registration owned by Fabrikam
A service principal (enterprise application) that Fabrikam's administrators can manage
A managed identity for the app
questions.explanation: There is only one application object, in Contoso's tenant. A service principal is created in every tenant that uses the app so that tenant's admins can control how it works there.

questions.q: A line-of-business app will be used only by employees and invited guests of your own tenant. Which supported account type should you choose?
options: Accounts in any organizational directory (multitenant)
Accounts in any organizational directory and personal Microsoft accounts
Personal Microsoft accounts only
Accounts in this organizational directory only (single tenant)
questions.explanation: Single tenant allows only users and guests from the tenant where the app is registered, which is the most common choice for line-of-business apps.

questions.q: A SaaS app must let users from any customer's Microsoft Entra tenant sign in with work or school accounts, but not personal Microsoft accounts. Which supported account type fits?
options: Accounts in this organizational directory only (single tenant)
Accounts in any organizational directory (multitenant)
Accounts in any organizational directory and personal Microsoft accounts
Personal Microsoft accounts only
questions.explanation: The multitenant option lets users from any Entra tenant sign in with their native identity. The other multitenant option additionally allows personal Microsoft accounts.

questions.q: A multitenant app must sign users in at their home tenants without an invitation process. Which endpoint should the app use?
options: The common or organizations endpoint
The tenant-specific endpoint of the developer's tenant
The Azure AD B2C endpoint
The device code endpoint only
questions.explanation: Using the common or organizations endpoint lets users sign in natively at their own tenants. A tenant-specific endpoint is used when signing in guests of a particular tenant.

questions.q: Which credential type does Microsoft recommend for production confidential client apps instead of client secrets?
options: Longer-lived client secrets that are rotated every 24 months
Passwords stored in app settings
Certificates, or federated identity credentials
Personal access tokens
questions.explanation: Microsoft says client secrets are less secure and shouldn't be used in production. Certificates are recommended, and federated credentials remove the need to manage secrets.

questions.q: A GitHub Actions workflow must authenticate to Microsoft Entra ID as an app without storing a secret or certificate. What should you configure?
options: A client secret with a long lifetime stored in the repository's encrypted secrets
A certificate stored in repository variables
A guest account for the workflow
A federated identity credential on the app registration
questions.explanation: Workload identity federation lets an external identity provider's token, such as GitHub's, be exchanged for an Entra token, so no secret has to be stored.

questions.q: A developer created a client secret but didn't save its value and can't find it. What should the developer do?
options: View the value again under Certificates & secrets
Create a new client secret, because the value is shown only once
Ask a Global Administrator to reveal the value from the app registration's audit log
Use the secret ID instead of the value
questions.explanation: The secret value is displayed only at creation. If it's lost, create a new secret, update the app and delete the old one. The secret ID isn't a usable credential.

questions.q: An administrator uploads a public key to an app registration under Certificates & secrets. Which file types are accepted?
options: .cer, .pem or .crt
.pfx only, because the private key must be uploaded to Microsoft Entra ID
.p12 or .pfx
.key or .jks
questions.explanation: You upload the public part of the certificate as .cer, .pem or .crt. The private key stays with the application.

questions.q: An app defines the roles Admin and Reader. How should you give users those roles?
options: Assign Microsoft Entra directory roles named Admin and Reader through Privileged Identity Management
Add the users as owners of the app registration
Define app roles on the app registration, then assign users or groups to them in the enterprise application's Users and groups
Grant delegated permissions named Admin and Reader
questions.explanation: App roles are defined on the application object and assigned to users, groups or applications through the service principal's Users and groups blade. They're unrelated to directory roles.

questions.q: A background service must read all mailboxes nightly with no signed-in user. Which permission type should it use?
options: Delegated permissions, consented to by each mailbox owner before the nightly job runs
Application permissions (app roles), granted by an administrator
Delegated permissions with user consent
Delegated permissions that a guest user grants
questions.explanation: App-only access uses application permissions that act without a user, and they always require admin consent. Delegated permissions need a signed-in user.

questions.q: Which type of permission always requires admin consent?
options: All delegated permissions
Delegated permissions for custom app scopes
The delegated User.Read permission
Application permissions (app roles)
questions.explanation: Application permissions have no user context, so only an administrator can consent to them. Many delegated permissions can be consented to by users.

questions.q: A non-administrator tries to consent to an app that requests the delegated permission User.Read.All and gets an error. What is the likely cause?
options: It is a high-privilege permission that requires admin consent
Delegated permissions never allow user consent, so every permission needs an administrator
The app isn't registered as multitenant
User.Read.All requires a user license
questions.explanation: Some high-privilege delegated permissions, such as User.Read.All, can only be consented to by an administrator. Users see a need admin approval prompt.

questions.q: What does a consent grant create for delegated permissions versus application permissions?
options: An app role assignment for delegated permissions, and an OAuth2 permission grant for application permissions
A service principal for both
An OAuth2 permission grant for delegated permissions, and an app role assignment for application permissions
A Conditional Access exclusion for both
questions.explanation: Delegated consent is recorded as an oAuth2PermissionGrant, while application permissions are recorded as an appRoleAssignment on the client's service principal.

questions.q: A developer wants to ask for extra permissions only when a feature is used, prompting just for the new permissions. Which consent model applies, and to which permissions?
options: Static consent, for both delegated and application permissions at sign-in time
Incremental (dynamic) consent, only for delegated permissions
Incremental consent, for application permissions only
Admin consent, for delegated permissions only
questions.explanation: Incremental or dynamic consent works only for delegated permissions. Application permissions are static and must be configured on the app registration.

questions.q: A consent request omits the resource in the scope parameter, for example scope=User.Read. Which API does the request target?
options: Azure Service Management
SharePoint Online
Azure AD Graph
Microsoft Graph
questions.explanation: When the resource identifier is omitted from the scope, the Microsoft identity platform defaults to Microsoft Graph, so User.Read means https://graph.microsoft.com/User.Read.

questions.q: Which delegated permissions are automatically included in the initial consent to an app because they're needed for basic functionality?
options: Signing in and reading the user's profile (User.Read), plus offline_access
Mail.Read and Calendars.Read
Directory.Read.All and Group.Read.All, which every app receives by default
Files.Read.All and Sites.Read.All
questions.explanation: The Sign you in and read your profile permission and offline_access are included automatically. Offline access provides refresh tokens, and the rest must be requested explicitly.

questions.q: An app requests a permission that needs admin consent dynamically through the scope parameter, but the permission isn't registered on the app registration. An admin tries to grant tenant-wide consent in the portal. What is the problem?
options: Dynamic consent can't be used with Microsoft Graph, so the portal rejects the grant
Admin consent is limited to application permissions
The portal's admin consent covers only permissions registered statically on the app registration
Tenant-wide consent requires the app to be publisher verified
questions.explanation: Admin consent on behalf of the organization uses the statically registered permissions, so the portal doesn't know about permissions requested dynamically. Configure them on the registration first.

questions.q: Which user consent setting does Microsoft recommend?
options: Allow user consent for apps
Allow user consent for apps from verified publishers, for selected permissions
Do not allow user consent and offer no admin consent workflow
Allow user consent for apps from any publisher after the user completes MFA
questions.explanation: Microsoft recommends letting users consent only to selected, lower-risk permissions for apps from verified publishers or apps registered in your tenant. Allowing all apps is the legacy behavior.

questions.q: Users see Need admin approval when they try to use a new app, and tenant administrators want users to be able to ask for approval. What should you enable?
options: A Conditional Access policy requiring terms of use
Access reviews on the enterprise application
Entitlement management access packages
The admin consent workflow
questions.explanation: The admin consent workflow lets users request consent for apps they can't consent to themselves, and designated reviewers handle the requests.

questions.q: You select Allow user consent for apps from verified publishers, for selected permissions. How do you define which permissions users may consent to?
options: Add delegated permissions to the Low permission classification
Add the permissions to a Conditional Access policy
Create an app role assignment for each user
Mark the permissions as admin-restricted in each app registration
questions.explanation: Permission classifications define which delegated permissions are low impact. Users can consent to those for apps from verified publishers or apps registered in the tenant.

questions.q: Under the verified publishers consent setting, an app from an unverified publisher outside your tenant requests only low-impact classified permissions. What happens?
options: Users can consent, because the permissions are low impact
The app is blocked automatically for administrators as well
Users can't consent, and administrator approval is required
Users can consent after completing MFA
questions.explanation: The setting requires both a qualifying app, meaning a verified publisher or an app registered in your tenant, and low-impact permissions. A non-qualifying app needs admin consent.

questions.q: You designate a user as a reviewer in the admin consent workflow, but the reviewer can't approve a request. What is the likely reason?
options: Reviewers can only be groups
Designating a reviewer doesn't elevate privileges, so the reviewer must also hold a role that can grant that consent
Reviewers need Entra ID P2 licenses and must be assigned the Security Reader role
Reviewers must be owners of the app
questions.explanation: A reviewer can only approve requests that their directory role permits. For example, granting some permissions requires Privileged Role Administrator.

questions.q: By default, after how many days does an admin consent request expire?
options: 7 days
14 days
90 days
30 days
questions.explanation: Consent requests expire after 30 days by default, and reviewers can receive reminders before expiry.

questions.q: An app requests Microsoft Graph application permissions. Which role is required to grant tenant-wide admin consent for them?
options: Privileged Role Administrator
Cloud Application Administrator
Application Administrator
Authentication Administrator
questions.explanation: Privileged Role Administrator can grant consent for any permission on any API. Cloud Application Administrator and Application Administrator can't grant Microsoft Graph application permissions.

questions.q: Which role is the least-privileged option in the list for granting tenant-wide admin consent to a third-party app that requests only delegated permissions?
options: Application Developer assigned at tenant scope
Cloud Application Administrator
Groups Administrator
Security Reader
questions.explanation: Cloud Application Administrator, Application Administrator and Privileged Role Administrator can grant tenant-wide consent for delegated permissions. Application Developer can register apps but not consent.

questions.q: What can happen when you grant tenant-wide admin consent to an application that already has tenant-wide grants?
options: Individual user grants are deleted, but tenant-wide grants are kept
All existing grants are merged without change
Previously granted tenant-wide permissions may be revoked, while permissions users granted for themselves aren't affected
The app's publisher verification is reset
questions.explanation: Granting tenant-wide consent can replace permissions that were already granted tenant-wide for the app. Permissions that users granted on their own behalf aren't affected.

questions.q: Finance needs an app, and an administrator grants tenant-wide consent. How do you ensure only the Finance group can use it?
options: Remove the admin consent and ask each user to consent individually
Set Visible to users to No
Add the Finance group as owners of the app
Set Assignment required to Yes and assign only the Finance group
questions.explanation: Consent is tenant-wide, but access isn't. With Assignment required enabled, only assigned users and groups can sign in. Hiding the app from My Apps doesn't block sign-in.

questions.q: Besides users, what does enabling Assignment required also restrict?
options: Service principals that use application permissions to get tokens for the app
Only guest users who were invited from other tenants
Access to the app registration blade
Reading the app's metadata
questions.explanation: The setting controls who or what can get a token for the application, so it also restricts apps that call it with application permissions unless they're assigned.

questions.q: You want an enterprise app to keep working but not appear in users' My Apps portal and Microsoft 365 launcher. What should you do?
options: Set Assignment required to Yes
Remove the app's logo
Set Visible to users to No
Disable Enabled for users to sign in
questions.explanation: Visible to users controls whether the app shows in My Apps and the launcher. It doesn't change who can sign in.

questions.q: Which user can sign in to an application regardless of its Assignment required setting?
options: A User Administrator
A Global Administrator
An application owner
A Cloud Application Administrator
questions.explanation: Users with the Global Administrator role can sign in to applications regardless of the assignment required setting.

questions.q: A suspicious app was granted consent by several users. You want to stop users from signing in to it immediately without deleting it. What should you do?
options: Delete the app registration, which removes the app from every tenant
Remove the app's owners
Grant tenant-wide admin consent
Set Enabled for users to sign in to No on the enterprise application
questions.explanation: Disabling sign-in on the enterprise application blocks users while keeping the object for investigation. Existing consent grants remain until revoked.

questions.q: After an OAuth consent phishing incident, you set user consent to Do not allow user consent. What happens to the grants users already gave?
options: They are removed automatically within 24 hours after the setting is saved
They remain in place, and you must revoke the existing grants explicitly
They are converted into admin consent
They stop working until users consent again
questions.explanation: Changing consent settings affects future consent only. Existing grants stay until revoked, so remove the malicious app's OAuth2 permission grants and disable the app.

questions.q: Which requirement is necessary for publisher verification?
options: A verified Cloud Partner Program (formerly Microsoft Partner Network) account whose Partner One ID is associated with the app
An Entra ID P2 license for the developer and a verified custom domain
A paid Microsoft support plan
Admin consent granted in every customer tenant
questions.explanation: Publisher verification uses a verified Cloud Partner Program account that is the partner global account, plus a matching publisher domain. No license is needed.

questions.q: A developer registered an app by using a personal Microsoft account and wants the blue verified badge. What is the outcome?
options: Possible after adding a verified domain to the app's publisher settings
Possible with an Entra ID P1 license
Not possible; apps registered with a Microsoft account can't be publisher verified
Possible only for single-tenant apps
questions.explanation: The app must be registered by using a Microsoft Entra work or school account to be publisher verified.

questions.q: What does publisher verification cost a developer?
options: An annual fee per app registration, billed through Azure
An Entra ID P2 license
A Microsoft 365 E5 license
Nothing; there is no charge and no license is required
questions.explanation: Microsoft doesn't charge for publisher verification, and developers who meet the prerequisites can be verified within minutes.

questions.q: What does the blue verified publisher badge indicate?
options: The app passed a Microsoft security audit and is certified for compliance
The publisher's identity was verified through its partner account, not the app's quality or security certification
The app complies with industry standards such as ISO 27001
The app requests only low-impact permissions
questions.explanation: The badge shows that the publisher verified its identity with Microsoft. It doesn't say anything about quality, certifications or the permissions requested.

questions.q: Developers in your tenant can't register applications, and you want to give a few users that ability with minimal privilege. Which role fits?
options: Application Developer
Application Administrator
Cloud Application Administrator
Privileged Role Administrator
questions.explanation: Application Developer is the least-privileged role that can create app registrations when the tenant setting restricts registration. The other roles are broader.

questions.q: A vendor's multitenant app isn't in your tenant yet, and you want to grant tenant-wide consent before any user signs in. What should you do?
options: Create an app registration with the same name and copy its client ID
Invite the vendor's developers as guests
Enable the admin consent workflow
Use the admin consent URL with the app's client ID, signed in as an authorized administrator
questions.explanation: If the client ID is known, you can build the tenant-wide admin consent URL. Signing in as an authorized admin provisions the service principal and grants consent.

questions.q: A user with limited access uses an app that holds the delegated permission Files.Read.All. What can the app read?
options: All files in the organization
No files unless the signed-in user is also an administrator
Only the files that the signed-in user can access
Only files the app created
questions.explanation: Delegated permissions let the app act as the signed-in user, so its effective access is limited to what both the app was granted and the user can do.
